decks.title: Fire and Ice — Robert Frost
goals: Explain the central idea of the poem in your own words
Explain the symbolism of fire (desire) and ice (hatred)
Identify symbolism, irony and understatement and say what they do
Describe the poem's form and rhyme scheme
Answer extract-based and 40–50 word questions on the poem

slides.heading: Fire and Ice — Robert Frost
slides.body_md:
*First Flight*, poetry · Class 10 CBSE English.

**Read the poem itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT), aloud, twice.** This lesson is SOYL's explanation; it does not reproduce the poem.

rows: an extract with short questions on meaning, tone and devices (answer A or B)

visual.alt: Table of how a First Flight poem is examined: a five-mark reference to context extract and three-mark short answers of forty to fifty words.
visual.caption: CBSE 2026-27, Section C (literature).

slides.narration: Welcome. Today’s poem is Fire and Ice by Robert Frost, the poet of Dust of Snow. It is only nine lines long, so please read it in First Flight now, aloud, twice. We will not repeat its lines here. Instead we will understand its argument, its two great symbols, its calm and ironic tone, and how to answer board questions on it.

slides.heading: How to read a very short poem
bullets: Read it aloud twice from *First Flight*; notice where the lines become short.
Ask: what question does the poem raise? what answer does the speaker give, and why?
Then ask: what might fire and ice stand for?
In answers, explain in your own words; never copy lines.
slides.narration: A nine line poem can carry a big idea, so read slowly. First read it aloud twice and notice where the lines suddenly become short. Then ask what question the poem raises, and what answer the speaker gives. Finally ask what fire and ice might stand for. In the exam, explain in your own words. Copying lines does not earn marks.

slides.heading: The poet: Robert Frost

rows: poems of New England country life, in plain everyday language with deeper meanings
Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, four times

visual.alt: Table of facts about Robert Frost: American poet, 1874 to 1963, known for New England poems in plain language, four-time Pulitzer Prize winner, also the poet of Dust of Snow; Fire and Ice appears in New Hampshire, 1923.

slides.narration: You met Robert Frost in Dust of Snow. He was an American poet who lived from eighteen seventy-four to nineteen sixty-three, and he wrote about country life in New England in plain language that hides deep ideas. He won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry four times. Fire and Ice was collected in his book New Hampshire, published in nineteen twenty-three.

slides.heading: The poem at a glance

rows: aba abc bcb: only three rhyme sounds
mostly moderate; three very short lines, including the last two
first person, judging from his own experience
how everything might finally be destroyed: by heat or by cold

visual.alt: Table of the poem at a glance: nine lines in one stanza, rhyme scheme a b a, a b c, b c b with three rhyme sounds, three very short lines including the last two, a first-person speaker, the subject of final destruction by heat or cold, and a calm, ironic tone.

slides.narration: Here is the poem at a glance. Nine lines, one stanza. The rhyme scheme is a b a, a b c, b c b, so only three rhyme sounds weave through it. Most lines are of moderate length, but three are very short, including the last two. The speaker talks in the first person. The subject is enormous: how everything might finally be destroyed. Yet the tone is calm.

slides.heading: The opening: an old question
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: the poem begins with a debate people have had for centuries. Will everything finally be destroyed by burning heat, or by freezing cold? Both answers are mentioned straight away.
slides.narration: The poem opens with an old debate. People have long wondered whether everything will finally be destroyed by burning heat or by freezing cold. Religious stories and scientific theories have offered both answers. Frost mentions the two opinions straight away, briefly, as if they were familiar to everyone. But he is about to give the question a very personal twist.

slides.heading: The speaker's first choice: fire
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: the speaker weighs the two opinions against his own life. He has known desire, and that knowledge makes him side with the people who expect fire.
slides.narration: Next the speaker judges the debate by his own experience. He describes desire as something he has tasted, as if he has sampled it like food. What he has learnt about desire makes him side with the people expecting a fiery end. Notice the move: a question about the earth has become a question about the human heart.

slides.heading: Check: what does fire stand for?
slides.narration: Your turn. The speaker links fire with something he has known in his own life. What does fire stand for in this poem? Choose the best answer.

slides.heading: The second ending: ice
slides.body_md: In SOYL's words: the speaker then imagines everything being destroyed a second time. His knowledge of hatred convinces him that ice would do that job just as well. He closes with a mild word meaning only that ice would be enough.
slides.narration: Then the speaker imagines a second destruction. If everything had to be destroyed again, he says in effect, he has seen so much hatred that he knows ice would work equally well. Ice stands for hatred. And he ends with a very mild word, one that simply means be enough. Hold on to that word; it is the key to the tone.

slides.heading: The speaker's argument

nodes.label: Two popular views: heat or cold
Ice would be just as effective

visual.alt: Flow of the speaker’s argument: two popular views, his experience with desire, he sides with fire, he imagines a second destruction, his knowledge of hatred, and his conclusion that ice would be just as effective.
visual.caption: The speaker's argument (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Here is the whole argument as a flow. Two popular views, heat or cold. The speaker recalls desire and sides with fire. Then he imagines a second destruction, recalls hatred, and concludes that ice would be just as effective. If you can explain these six steps in your own words, you can answer almost any question on the poem.

slides.heading: Symbols: fire and ice
slides.body_md: Fire and ice begin as physical forces and become symbols of two human emotions.

rows: consumes everything it reaches; wars over land, wealth, power
freezes sympathy; cracks families, communities, nations

visual.alt: Table of the two symbols: fire stands for desire, sharing heat, speed and endless hunger, and destroys by consuming; ice stands for hatred, sharing coldness, hardness and slowness, and destroys by freezing sympathy and cracking relationships.

slides.narration: Why fire for desire? Fire is hot and fast, it spreads to everything near it, and it is never satisfied. Greed, lust and ambition behave the same way. Why ice for hatred? Ice, by contrast, feels cold, hard and slow. It numbs and cracks. Hatred freezes sympathy and slowly breaks families and nations apart. Two opposite forces, one result: destruction.

slides.heading: Fire versus ice
columns:
**Fire: desire**

- hot, quick, fierce
- greed for money, land, power
- grows the more it is fed
- destroys by consuming

**Ice: hatred**

- cold, slow, silent
- grudges, prejudice, indifference
- hardens over time
- destroys by freezing and cracking
slides.narration: Set the two side by side. Fire is hot, quick and fierce, like greed for money, land or power, which grows the more it is fed. Ice, by contrast, feels cold, slow and silent, like grudges, prejudice and indifference, which harden over time. They work in opposite ways, yet the speaker treats them as equally dangerous. That is the heart of the poem.

slides.heading: Check: assertion and reason
slides.narration: Check yourself with an assertion and reason. Both statements may be true, but does the second really explain the first? Think about what actually convinces the speaker that ice could destroy everything.

slides.heading: Themes and message
bullets: **Human emotions are the real danger:** desire and hatred, not comets or frozen ages.
**Opposites can destroy equally:** hot desire and cold hatred lead to the same end.
**Experience as evidence:** the speaker trusts what he has felt.
**A warning, not a sermon:** the poem lets readers draw their own conclusion.
slides.narration: The themes follow. Human emotions are the real danger, not natural disasters. Opposite feelings, hot desire and cold hatred, can destroy equally. The speaker trusts his own experience as evidence. And the poem is a warning, not a sermon; it lets us draw the conclusion. In answers, state a theme and support it with the symbols.

slides.heading: Poetic devices, with SOYL's own examples
slides.body_md: Each device is described in the poem and illustrated with a SOYL sentence, not with the poem's lines.

aba abc bcb, three interlocking sounds

visual.alt: Table of poetic devices in the poem, described, each with a SOYL example: symbolism, metaphor, contrast, understatement, irony and an interlocking rhyme scheme.

slides.narration: Now the devices. Symbolism, in fire and ice. A metaphor, as desire is something tasted. Contrast, hot against cold. Understatement, a mild word for total destruction. Irony, a calm voice on a terrifying subject. And an interlocking rhyme scheme. The examples in the right column are our own sentences, written to show each device.

slides.heading: Understatement and irony at the close
slides.body_md: The poem ends with a modest word meaning *be enough*, applied to the destruction of everything. Read the ending aloud in *First Flight* and notice how flat and quiet it sounds.
bullets: **What is said:** ice would be enough.
**What is meant:** hatred could wipe out everything.
**The gap:** a tiny word for a vast catastrophe is understatement; the mismatch creates irony.
**Effect:** the ending sounds calm, and that calm is chilling.
slides.narration: Here is a worked point you can use in answers. The poem ends with a modest word that simply means be enough, applied to the destruction of everything. What is said is small; what is meant is huge. That gap is understatement, and the mismatch creates irony. The calm makes the ending chilling, as if the speaker had already accepted the danger.

slides.heading: Tone
slides.body_md: Calm, casual and conversational, almost like a person giving an opinion over tea. The subject is catastrophe; the voice never rises. That mismatch is the source of the poem's irony and its chill.
slides.narration: Listen to the tone. The speaker sounds calm and casual, almost like someone giving an opinion over a cup of tea. Yet the subject is the end of everything. His voice never rises. That mismatch between a gentle voice and a terrible subject is the source of the irony, and it is why the poem feels so chilling.

slides.heading: Word meanings

visual.alt: Table of word meanings: desire, hate, perish, destruction and suffice.
visual.caption: Single words from the poem with their meanings.

slides.narration: A few words to know. Desire, strong wanting or craving. Hate, intense dislike. Perish, to die or be destroyed. Destruction, complete ruin. And suffice, to be enough. Students often confuse suffice with suffer, so learn it well. It is the most important word in the poem for questions on tone.

slides.heading: Check: the rhyme scheme
slides.narration: Quick check. Write the rhyme scheme of the poem using letters. Look in your textbook at which line endings share a sound. There are only three sounds in all.

slides.heading: Worked example: a 40–50 word answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* Why does the speaker believe that both fire and ice could destroy everything?
bullets: **Point:** both forces stand for powerful human emotions.
**Symbols:** fire is desire, which consumes; ice stands for hatred, which freezes and divides.
**Support:** he judges from his own experience of both feelings.

**Model (47 words):** *The speaker treats fire and ice as symbols. Fire is desire, which consumes everything and is never satisfied; ice represents hatred, which freezes sympathy and breaks people apart. Having known both feelings himself, he believes either emotion, left unchecked, could bring about total destruction.*

visual.alt: Flow for a forty to fifty word answer: find the key word, state the point, explain the symbol and its meaning, add the effect or message.

slides.narration: Here is how to build a three mark answer. Find the key word: both. State the point: the forces stand for emotions. Explain each symbol: fire is desire, ice stands for hatred. Add support: his own experience. The model is forty-seven words, inside the limit, and it does not copy a single line of the poem.

slides.heading: Check: the last word
slides.narration: One more. The poem’s final word is suffice. What does it mean? It tells you how calmly the speaker sums up the power of hatred.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Opening: two old views, destruction by heat or by cold.
Fire = desire; the speaker's experience makes him side with it.
Ice = hatred; it would be just as effective a second time.
Form: 9 lines, one stanza, aba abc bcb; short final lines; understatement and irony.
Message: uncontrolled human emotions are the real threat. Read the poem in *First Flight*.

nodes.label: Two popular views: heat or cold
Ice would be just as effective

visual.alt: Flow of the speaker’s argument: two popular views, his experience with desire, he sides with fire, he imagines a second destruction, his knowledge of hatred, and his conclusion that ice would be just as effective.
visual.caption: The speaker's argument (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Let us sum up. The poem opens with two old views, heat or cold. Fire stands for desire, and the speaker’s experience makes him side with it. Ice stands for hatred, which would be just as effective. Nine lines, one stanza, three rhyme sounds, and a mild final word that creates understatement and irony. The message: our own emotions are the real threat.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Never write out the poem's lines; explain the idea in your own words.
Always give the symbolic meaning: fire = desire, ice = hatred.
Name devices **and** say what they do: *the mild last word understates total destruction, creating irony*.
40–50 word answers: point + symbol + effect or message.
Common slips: reading the poem only literally; saying the speaker rejects fire; *suffice* as "suffer".
slides.narration: Exam tips. Never write out the lines; explain in your own words. Always give the symbolic meaning, fire for desire and ice for hatred. When you name a device, say what it does. Keep three mark answers to point, symbol and effect. And avoid the common slips: the poem is not only literal, the speaker does not reject fire, and suffice does not mean suffer.

notes.title: Fire and Ice — study notes

sections.heading: 1. The poet and the poem
sections.body_md:
**Read the poem itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT), aloud, twice.** This lesson is SOYL's explanation; it does not reproduce the poem.

**Robert Frost** (1874–1963) was an American poet who wrote about country life in New England in plain, everyday language with deeper meanings. He won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry four times. *Fire and Ice* is a short lyric collected in *New Hampshire* (1923); his *Dust of Snow* is Chapter 13 of your book.

rows: poems of New England country life, in plain everyday language with deeper meanings
Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, four times

visual.alt: Table of facts about Robert Frost: American poet, 1874 to 1963, known for New England poems in plain language, four-time Pulitzer Prize winner, also the poet of Dust of Snow; Fire and Ice appears in New Hampshire, 1923.

sections.heading: 2. What the poem says (SOYL summary)
sections.body_md:
**The opening:** the poem begins with an old debate: will everything finally be destroyed by burning heat or by freezing cold?

**The first choice:** judging from his own experience with desire, the speaker sides with the people who expect fire.

**The second ending:** he then imagines a second destruction and, from what he knows of hatred, concludes that ice would be just as effective. He ends with a mild word meaning *be enough*.

The poem is spoken in the first person and moves from a cosmic question to the human heart.

nodes.label: Two popular views: heat or cold
Ice would be just as effective

visual.alt: Flow of the speaker’s argument: two popular views, his experience with desire, he sides with fire, he imagines a second destruction, his knowledge of hatred, and his conclusion that ice would be just as effective.
visual.caption: The speaker's argument (SOYL summary).

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Human emotions are the real danger:** desire and hatred, left unchecked, can destroy individuals and civilisations.
- **Opposites can destroy equally:** hot, fast desire and cold, slow hatred lead to the same end.
- **Experience as evidence:** the speaker trusts what he has felt, not what experts say.
- **A warning, not a sermon:** the poem offers no cure; the reader draws the conclusion.

sections.heading: 4. Symbols, devices and form
sections.body_md:
**Fire:** desire (greed, lust, ambition, craving): hot, spreading, never satisfied. **Ice:** hatred (coldness, indifference, rigidity): cold, slow, numbing, cracking.

**Devices:** symbolism; metaphor (desire as something tasted); contrast or antithesis (hot vs cold); understatement (a mild last word for total destruction); irony (a calm voice on a terrifying subject).

**Form:** nine lines in a single stanza; rhyme scheme aba abc bcb (three interlocking sounds); mostly moderate lines with three very short ones, including the last two, which slow the ending.

key_terms.definition_md: An object that stands for an idea (fire for desire).
Saying something deliberately less strongly than the facts deserve.
A gap between what is said and what is meant, or between tone and subject.

sections.body_md: Calm, casual and conversational. The speaker discusses the end of everything as if giving an everyday opinion. The mismatch between the gentle voice and the terrible subject creates irony, and the mild final word makes the ending chilling rather than dramatic.

sections.heading: 7. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**Extract-based (5 marks):** the board prints the poem's lines; SOYL practice uses commentary passages instead. Expect questions on meaning, symbols, tone, devices and the rhyme scheme.

**Short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words):** point + symbol and its meaning + effect or message.

Practise with the poem itself in *First Flight*; never reproduce its lines in an answer.

visual.alt: Flow for a forty to fifty word answer: find the key word, state the point, explain the symbol and its meaning, add the effect or message.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** reference-to-context extract (5) and short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words) on First Flight poems (CBSE 2026-27, Section C).

**How marks are awarded:** a correct point, support from the poem in your own words, and accurate expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Writing out the poem instead of explaining it.
2. Explaining fire and ice only literally, without desire and hatred.
3. Saying the speaker rejects fire and chooses ice.
4. Reading *suffice* as *suffer*.
5. Naming understatement or irony without saying what it does.

**Remember:** read the poem in your textbook, *First Flight*.

questions.stem_md: Read the commentary on *Fire and Ice* and answer the questions that follow. *(This passage is SOYL's commentary on the poem, not lines from it. Read the poem itself in your textbook, First Flight.)*
questions.solution_md: Answer from the commentary; parts (a) and (c) also follow from your reading of the poem.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) by heat and by cold

**(b)** heart

**(c)** (d) His real subject is human feeling, not science.

**(d)** A familiar debate draws readers in at once, and he can then give it a surprising, personal twist.

questions.passage_md: Frost opens his poem in the middle of an old argument. People have long wondered how everything will finally be destroyed, and the poem sets out the two popular answers almost at once: destruction by heat, or destruction by cold. Scientists and religious thinkers had offered both answers. But the poet is not really interested in astronomy or prophecy. Within a few lines he moves the question inside the human heart, where heat and cold become two feelings that can wreck lives as surely as any comet or frozen age.

children.stem_md: Which two ways of destruction does the opening of *Fire and Ice* set out?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** by heat and by cold. The poem begins with the two popular answers: heat (fire) and cold (ice).

children.stem_md: The commentary says the poet moves the question inside the human ___.
children.solution_md: He moves it inside the human **heart**: fire and ice become feelings.

children.stem_md: What does the commentary mean when it says Frost is not really interested in astronomy?

options.text_md: He knew nothing about the stars.
He wanted to write a science textbook.
His real subject is human feeling, not science.

children.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** His real subject is human feeling, not science. The cosmic question is only a starting point; the poem is about emotions.

children.stem_md: Why might Frost begin *Fire and Ice* with a question many people had already argued about?
children.solution_md: A known question hooks the reader before the poem turns it inward.

answer.model_answer_md: A familiar debate draws readers in at once, and he can then give it a surprising, personal twist.

marking_scheme.step: Familiar question hooks the reader; then a twist

children.stem_md: According to the commentary, how quickly does the poem set out the two answers?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** almost at once. The commentary says the two answers appear almost at once.

questions.stem_md: Read the commentary on *Fire and Ice* and answer the questions that follow. *(This passage is SOYL's commentary on the poem, not lines from it. Read the poem itself in your textbook, First Flight.)*
questions.solution_md: Link fire to desire, then explain which qualities they share.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) his own experience with desire

**(b)** desire

**(c)** (c) It is never satisfied and keeps spreading.

**(d)** That he has known desire personally and found how strongly it can grip a person.

**(e)** (a) Two neighbours fight for years over a strip of land each wants.

questions.passage_md: The speaker does not consult books or experts before choosing a side. He consults his own experience. He describes desire as something he has sampled, the way one samples food, and what he has learnt from it makes him side with the people who expect a fiery end. Fire is a fitting picture for desire: it is hot, it spreads quickly, and it is never satisfied, consuming whatever it touches and then looking for more. Greed for money, land or power behaves in just this way, and so does unchecked ambition.

children.stem_md: On what does the speaker of *Fire and Ice* base his first choice?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** his own experience with desire. He relies on his own experience, not on experts.

children.stem_md: In the poem, fire stands for ___.
children.solution_md: Fire symbolises **desire** (greed, passion, ambition).

children.stem_md: Which quality of fire, named in the commentary, makes it a good symbol for desire?

options.text_md: It is cold to the touch.
It is never satisfied and keeps spreading.
It is easy to see through.

children.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is never satisfied and keeps spreading. Like desire, fire consumes and then looks for more.

children.stem_md: What does the speaker's way of describing desire, as something sampled like food, suggest?
children.solution_md: The image of tasting shows first-hand experience.

answer.model_answer_md: That he has known desire personally and found how strongly it can grip a person.

children.stem_md: Which situation best shows the kind of fire the commentary describes?

options.text_md: Two neighbours fight for years over a strip of land each wants.
A child shares lunch with a friend.
A farmer waits for the rain.
A student helps a classmate revise.

children.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Two neighbours fight for years over a strip of land each wants. Greed for land that keeps growing into conflict is desire acting like fire.

questions.stem_md: Read the commentary on *Fire and Ice* and answer the questions that follow. *(This passage is SOYL's commentary on the poem, not lines from it. Read the poem itself in your textbook, First Flight.)*
questions.solution_md: Explain ice as hatred and show how the speaker treats it as an equal danger.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) hatred

**(b)** (b) when he imagines the earth being destroyed a second time

**(c)** numbs

**(d)** It makes people cold and indifferent (it freezes sympathy).

**(e)** (a) as equally capable

questions.passage_md: Having chosen fire, the speaker pauses to imagine a second ending. If the earth had to be destroyed one more time, he says in effect, hatred would do the job just as well. Ice makes a cold, quiet destroyer. It does not blaze; it hardens, numbs and cracks. Hatred works the same way: it makes people cold and indifferent to one another, it freezes sympathy, and over time it can break families, communities and nations. The speaker knows hatred well enough to judge its power, and he does not rank it below desire.

children.stem_md: In *Fire and Ice*, what does ice stand for?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** hatred. Ice symbolises hatred: coldness and indifference.

children.stem_md: When does the speaker think about ice as a destroyer?

options.text_md: before he mentions fire at all
when he imagines the earth being destroyed a second time
when he gives up his first choice

children.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** when he imagines the earth being destroyed a second time. He keeps fire as his first choice and imagines a second destruction by ice.

children.stem_md: The commentary says ice does not blaze; instead it hardens, ___ and cracks.
children.solution_md: Ice hardens, **numbs** and cracks, as hatred does.

children.stem_md: Give one way in which hatred, according to the commentary, works like ice.
children.solution_md: Any one: coldness, indifference, frozen sympathy, slow breaking of ties.

answer.model_answer_md: It makes people cold and indifferent (it freezes sympathy).

marking_scheme.step: Any one valid likeness from the commentary

children.stem_md: How does the speaker rank hatred compared with desire as a destroyer?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** as equally capable. He does not rank it below desire: ice would do the job just as well.

questions.passage_md: The poem is tiny, a single stanza of nine lines, yet it is tightly built. Only three rhyme sounds run through it, interlocking in the pattern aba abc bcb, so that each new rhyme is introduced before the old one is dropped. Most lines are of a similar, moderate length, but three are very short, and the last two of these close the poem. answer.model_answer_md:
Small Fires, Slow Ice

Robert Frost's poem Fire and Ice warns that desire and hatred can destroy humanity. The same forces work on a smaller scale in our school. Fire appears as unhealthy competition: the craving to top every test, to own the latest phone or to win at any cost. It can turn friends into rivals. Ice appears as grudges, cold silences and groups that exclude others. Nobody shouts, yet friendships slowly freeze. questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of the speaker's argument in *Fire and Ice* in order (SOYL summary).

options.text_md: He concludes that ice would be just as effective.
He sides with the people expecting fire.
The speaker recalls his experience with desire.
He recalls what he knows of hatred.
Two popular opinions about the final destruction are mentioned.
He imagines everything being destroyed a second time.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (c) → (b) → (f) → (d) → (a). Two views → desire → fire → a second destruction → hatred → ice would work too.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps for writing a 40–50 word answer on the symbols of *Fire and Ice*.

options.text_md: Explain one quality each symbol shares with its emotion.
Read the question and underline its key word.
Check the word count and remove any quoted lines.
Add the effect or the message.
Name what fire and ice stand for.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). Understand the question → name the symbols → explain the link → add the message → check length and originality.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Match each word used in *Fire and Ice* with its meaning.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Single words from the poem with their meanings.

questions.stem_md: Match each element of *Fire and Ice* with what it stands for or suggests.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(r), (c)–(q), (d)–(p). Fire and ice are symbols; the experience and the last word explain how the speaker reaches and states his view.

options.text_md: desire described as something sampled like food
a mild word for the end of everything
hot and cold forces set side by side

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(q), (d)–(s). Name the device by what it does in the poem.
